name: North Carolina
overview: North Carolina counties do not sell tax lien certificates; they collect delinquent property taxes by foreclosing on the land and selling the property itself. A county can foreclose either through a court action in the nature of a mortgage foreclosure, where the judgment appoints a commissioner who sells the property by public auction to the highest bidder, or through the in rem method, where the tax collector files a certificate with the clerk of superior court and the sheriff sells the property like other real property sold under execution. After the auction the high bid stays open for upset bids: anyone may raise it by at least five percent, with a minimum increase of $750, and each upset bid starts a new 10-day period. Once the sale is confirmed the commissioner delivers the deed on payment of the price, and the buyer takes the property free and clear of most claims; the owner can stop the foreclosure by paying before the sale is confirmed, but there is no redemption period after it.

counties.how_to_bid: Bid in person at the auction held by the Orange County Sheriff's Department on the Orange County Courthouse steps, 106 E. Margaret Lane, Hillsborough. Sales are advertised for two weeks beforehand in the News of Orange or the Chapel Hill Herald. The highest bidder pays the full bid amount at the end of the sale (not a deposit) in cash or certified funds payable to the Orange County Sheriff's Department, plus excise tax and recording fees. A ten-day upset bid period follows, filed with the Orange County Clerk of Court by 5:00 p.m. on the tenth day after the Report of Sale is filed; an upset bid must be at least 5% higher and not less than $750, in cash or certified funds. If no upset bid is filed, the sale is confirmed and the Sheriff delivers a non-warranty Sheriff's Deed. Properties are sold as is. Registration steps are not stated.

counties.how_to_bid: Harnett County mainly uses the mortgage-style foreclosure method, so a court-appointed commissioner sells at public auction on the Harnett County Courthouse steps (or another place the Clerk of Court designates). Notices are posted at the courthouse at least 20 days before the sale and published in The Daily Record once a week for two weeks. The opening bid covers the taxes, fees and costs. The winning bidder pays a deposit; the page gives two figures (10% of the bid in the procedures section, and 5% or $750, whichever is greater, in certified funds or cash in the law firm section). Upset bids of at least 5% or $750 more, whichever is greater, may be filed during a 10-day period that restarts with each upset bid. After confirmation the balance is due (the page says no more than 20 days in one place and two to three weeks in another) and the buyer receives a Commissioner's Deed. Properties are sold as is, where is; the owner may redeem before confirmation. Sale time varies by sale.

counties.how_to_bid: The Henderson County Sheriff's Department conducts the sale at the front door of the Courthouse, 200 N. Grove Street, Hendersonville. Arrive early: there is a short registration process for all bidders on the day of the sale. The highest bidder pays a 10% cash deposit at the close of bidding. Anyone may upset the bid within 10 days by raising it 5% of the last reported price or upset bid, and by no less than $750, filed with the Clerk of Superior Court; the full upset bid must be paid in cash before the period expires. The successful bidder receives a Sheriff's Deed, which the bidder must record with the Register of Deeds. The estimated opening bid does not include interest and expenses that keep accruing. Sale time is not stated.
